en: The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Aśokadatta, Daughter of King Ajātaśatru, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, together with [the assembly of] monks...

He addressed the assembly of five hundred bhikṣus and eight thousand bodhisattvas—each one most venerable and honored—who had all attained the *dhāraṇī* dharmas; in whatever they heard or knew, they were like the great ocean, free from all obstruction. They had all attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and deeply entered subtle and wondrous *upāyakauśalya*. They held the treasury-gate of the dharma of emptiness, never abandoning their resolve, practicing the perception of formlessness, and acting according to the Dharma without any place of reliance, nor performing any conditioned actions. In preaching the sūtra-dharma, they were without attachment; for the sake of all beings, they contemplated their own fundamental nature and, having attained patience, practiced ten matters in total.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Sumeru; furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Mahāsumeru;
furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Sumeruśikhara; furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Siṃha; furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Vahamaī;
furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Nityotkṣiptahasta; furthermore, there was a bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva named Constantly Lowering the Hand; furthermore, there was a Bodhisattva named Constantly Diligent Practice;
furthermore, there was a Bodhisattva named Constant Joy; furthermore, there was a Bodhisattva named Constantly Concerned for All People;
furthermore, there was a Bodhisattva named Precious Mindfulness; furthermore, there was a Bodhisattva named Precious Hand; furthermore, there was a Bodhisattva named...
Ratnamudrāhasta; furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Yantṛ,
another named Mahāyantṛ, another named Satyadhara, and another named Maitreya—
these and others, seventeen in all.
The eight persons, including Ānanda and others, were all of the same class as Ānanda:

the Bodhisattva Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Ratnapūrṇa, the Bodhisattva Kautūhala, the Bodhisattva Indradatta, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāraṇa, the Bodhisattva Nityasmṛti, the Bodhisattva Lokahitasmṛti, and the Bodhisattva Lokapuṇyavardhana—these were the eight.

At that time, the Buddha was together with eight thousand bodhisattvas, staying not far from the city of Rājagṛha; he was honored, revered, praised, and regarded like a father by kings and ministers, and was held in high esteem by brahmins and householders.

At that time, the Buddha preached the Dharma among an immeasurable great assembly—the words he spoke were excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; there was nothing in his teaching that did not bring forth realization, as he clearly understood all things superior, middling, and inferior, which were entirely complete, unsullied, and infinitely energetic.

At that time, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Pūrṇa, Rāhula, Lohitya, Ānanda, Upāli, and others—countless great bhikṣus from various regions beyond measure—dressed themselves properly at dawn, took their alms bowls, and entered the great city of Rājagṛha for alms.

This venerable bhikṣu entered the city and proceeded through the streets and alleys for alms; eventually arriving at the palace of King Ajātaśatru, where the palace ladies and court officials were gathered together, he silently begged for alms from them.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru had a daughter named Āśokā (translated into Chinese as Wuchouyou, "Free from Sorrow"), twelve years of age, who was upright, beautiful, and pure, possessing the foremost complexion. Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, she possessed a spirit of fierce resolve; she had made offerings to countless Buddhas and her mind never wavered from the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. She sat peacefully upon a golden couch in the main hall of her father, the king.

Seeing this venerable bhikṣu, Aśoka felt no sorrow; he did not move from his father the king’s main hall, nor did he rise from his seat, nor go forward to meet him, nor pay him homage, nor invite him to sit, nor provide him with alms-requisites.
The venerable bhikṣus also remained silent as they gazed at this woman.
When King Ajātaśatru saw that the woman Viśākhā was neither distressed nor did she pay respectful homage to these venerable bhikṣus, the king turned to her and said:
"Do you not know?"

This venerable bhikṣu, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having attained arhatship, has nothing further to fear; his deeds are preeminent, he has cast off the heavy burden, severed the cycle of birth and death, and has entered deeply into the subtle and wondrous.
The merit of making offerings to such a person is immeasurable; they act as teacher and father, giving rise to compassionate thoughts and bestowing blessings upon all.
For what reason do you not rise from your seat when seeing him, but instead remain silent and gaze at him?
"What special benefit do you have that you do not pay homage to this Most Honorable One?
The woman Viśākhā replied:
"Has Your Majesty ever seen a lion prostrate before, welcome, or sit in the presence of some minor bird or beast?"
The king replied to the girl,
“I do not see it.
The girl spoke again:
"Have you ever heard, O King, that when a Cakravartin king arises as a minor king, he rises to meet him, pays homage, and sits together with him?
Or does Śakra Devānām Indra rise to meet the various devas and pay them homage?"
"Brahmasaṃpatti, do you pay homage to the various Brahmās?
He replied, "I do not."
The woman spoke again:
"Has Your Majesty ever seen the deity of the great ocean prostrate before small ponds, ditches, or springs?
Does Mount Sumeru ever prostrate before the various smaller mountains?"
"Is the radiance of the sun and moon equal to the light of a firefly?
The woman replied again,
"It is so, Great King!"

Having resolved to seek the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, desiring to deliver all beings, donning the great armor of *saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*, and maintaining great compassion and great pity like the lion’s roar—how could one be a monk who fears, yet lacks great compassion, great kindness, and great pity, and remains apart from the lion’s roar?
"How should one pay homage with faith and joy?

Have you ever seen the Great Dharma King turning the wheel of the sutras and treatises, teaching all beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Should one not respectfully prostrate before such a bhikṣu of even modest wisdom?"
The woman said to the king:
"Just as the waters of the great ocean cannot be measured, cannot be fathomed, and its limits cannot be seen—
how is it that one of such great wisdom as this still receives the flow from a spring?"
If one were to consider the water in a cow’s footprint as sufficient in itself, could it ever be compared to the great ocean?
Likewise, how could a bhikṣu who fears birth and death and whose resolve is set solely on nirvāṇa ever welcome and pay homage to one who has resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

Your Majesty has already seen that the Tathāgata’s Dharma is the most honored and supreme—like Mount Sumeru, the highest and most majestic. How much more so, then, should a bhikṣu whose wisdom is like a mustard seed not rise to meet him and pay homage?

"O King, you may indeed see the light of the sun and moon, yet the extent of their illumination is immeasurable; however, the radiance of the Dharma of the Tathāgata, as well as his wisdom, merit, and renown, surpasses these by thousands of billions of times. How can this be compared to the light of a firefly that merely illuminates its own body, failing to reach all people?"
“Those bhikṣus of small aspirations seek only their own deliverance; the Dharma of Great Wisdom illuminates the three realms—how could one possibly go out to meet them and pay them homage?
The woman said to the king:
“Even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one would not pay homage to such bhikṣus; how much less so while the Buddha is currently present as the standard for the Dharma?”
Why is this? Because by paying homage to that bhikṣu, one practices this Dharma; through such association, one attains the qualities of a Samyaksaṃbuddha and achieves the practice of Samyaksaṃbodhi.
The king said to the woman:
"Do not grieve! You possess a defiant mind;

upon seeing this great bhikṣu, you failed to welcome him with respect, instead treating the seating arrangement as if it were between host and guest, and though you cited many parables at length, you did not think to prepare a meal."
"What do you seek?
The woman said to the king,
"Great King, do you perhaps harbor a mind of aggression?"
The woman said to the king,
"For what reason does Your Majesty not pay homage to those in the kingdom who are weak, lowly, and destitute?
The king replied to the woman:
"Not so; this is not of my kind," the woman replied to the king, "It is even so, O King!"
"Bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment] are not of the same class as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The King said to the girl:

"I have heard that those who practice the Dharma of a Bodhisattva completely cast aside arrogance and anger, becoming harmonious and gentle, and humbling themselves before all people; do you, then, lack a gentle heart?"
The woman said to the king:

"Because the people of the world are ignorant and constantly harbor poisonous and evil minds, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva protects them with compassion and mercy, wishing to eliminate all their poisons."
"These great bhikṣus have already eliminated all defilements; such bhikṣus do not increase when they see the good, nor do they decrease when they see the evil.
The woman said to the king:
"Even if the Buddhas of the ten directions were to preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for these bhikṣus, they would be unable to further increase their diligence."
Why is this? Because it blocks the path of birth and death.
It is like a bottle filled to the brim with water placed in the open air; when it rains, not a single drop is received by the bottle, nor can a drop enter it.
"Why is this? Because the jar is full.
The woman said to the king:

“Such as these bhikṣus are, even if the Buddhas of the ten directions were to manifest miraculous transformations for them or preach the Dharma to them, they would be unable to attain the samādhi of the Tathāgata, nor would they gain any increase in merit.”
The woman said to the king:
“It is like the great ocean; the ten thousand streams flowing from the four directions all return to the sea. Why is this so? Because—”
That ocean is vast and long, and that which it receives is immeasurable.

In this same way, Great King, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva preaches the Dharma, it should be viewed as such: it brings great benefit, gives rise to the mind of Mahāyāna, and is capable of containing much.
"Why is this? Because the vessel of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva can receive that which is incalculable, innumerable, and immeasurable.
At that time, the woman Aśoka spoke these verses to King Ajātaśatru:
"Named Aśokā because I have attained freedom from sorrow, I am the daughter of King Ajātaśatru.
When five hundred bhikṣus arrived, I did not rise to greet them nor offer them salutation."
At that time, the king rebuked him, saying:
"You show no respect for the community of bhikṣus.
I did not know this was a field of merit; the Son of the Buddha has departed from its traces.
Free from sorrow, recite these verses: "Listen to my words of utmost sincerity.
Seeing a bhikṣu, you do not rise; no desire arises in your mind to pay him homage."
A person wishing to board a ship to enter the sea takes one coin and breaks it into a hundred parts;
from those hundred parts, they take one part, and upon entering the ocean of the Dharma, they do so for the sake of further taking.
If someone begs from a king, or even from a flying Cakravartin,
a beggar who seeks but a single coin will find it insufficient and thus begs from the king.
The wise bring joy to the king; from the king they beg for billions of jewels, wishing to bestow them upon the poor so that they may find peace and security—such a person is truly enlightened.
Just as a person who seeks base treasures is unwise, so too it is with the Dharma of the Śrāvakas;
they enter the ocean for jewels but take only a small portion for themselves.
Just as a person is wealthy through riches, so the Bodhisattva regards wisdom as his precious treasure;
may he offer worship to the Dharma King, thereby attaining Buddhahood himself and delivering all beings.
Just as a physician who treats only his own body cannot heal all people;
whereas a physician who treats many people is considered a renowned master of medicine.
One who has resolved their mind upon wisdom is a teacher;
though they have liberated themselves and abandoned others, they are not respected by the clever, just as a physician who can only heal himself.
But if a wise master knows the names of medicines, he is able to heal billions of people.
Respected by all people in the world—such is the bodhisattva who has resolved his mind.
Like a tree without leaves or fruit, which provides no benefit to the people of the world;
such is the arhat-tree, which provides no benefit to the world.
Just as the sandalwood tree Is beneficial to all people;
So too is the Dharma of the Bodhisattva, Opening the nectar of the sutras.
One cannot wash away the impurities and heat of a person with the water of a cow’s footprint;
yet the Ganges purifies countless people, and the waters of the Ganges flow to fill the great ocean.
The Dharma of the Śrāvakas is like water in a cow’s footprint, unable to remove the heat of the world;
the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas is like the waters of the Ganges, able to satisfy the entire trichiliocosm.
For example, when precious jewels fall like timely rain, the fool takes but a single coin;
yet the wise and discerning take much more, enabling them to rise from poverty to great wealth.
The Buddha is like one who rains down precious jewels;
the śrāvakas take but a single coin, while the bodhisattvas gather enough to satisfy all people. The generosity of the bodhisattva is thus vast.
Just as when someone approaches Mount Sumeru, they all take on a golden hue according to the mountain;
yet other mountains of earth and stone cannot transform their appearance with such color.

The Bodhisattva’s Dharma is like Mount Sumeru; through the Bodhisattva’s grace, one is born in the heavens and attains liberation from the suffering of birth and death—something a Śrāvaka cannot achieve in delivering others.
When dew is sparse upon the grass, it cannot ripen the five grains;
when the great rains provide abundant moisture, one obtains bountiful harvests from that moisture.
The Dharma of the Śrāvakas is like grass exposed to the sun; the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas is like a great rain.
To all who have come from throughout the great trichiliocosm, the rain of the Dharma moistens them all.
The *kāśī* flower has no fragrance, and thus it is not taken by the people of the world;
the *pāṭalī*, the *campaka*, the *udumbara*, and the lotus are what they delight in taking.
The *kāsīsa* flower of the śrāvaka-dharma has fragrance that does not travel far;
the *pāṭala* flower of the bodhisattva-dharma delivers all beings to nirvāṇa.
As when a timid person travels through a desolate wilderness, it is not yet considered a great peril;
but to travel the Middle Way among men is a great peril, for it leads all beings across birth and death.
The Dharma-practice of the Śrāvakas is like walking through an empty wilderness;
the Dharma-practice of the Bodhisattvas is within the path of humanity, delivering those bewildered by birth and death, and guiding all who are filled with fear.
A bound raft floats across but not far; a raft cannot carry one back and forth.
It is like a person who builds a great ship, able to cross over countless beings and travel to and fro.
The Dharma of the śrāvakas is like a bound raft;
the Dharma of the bodhisattvas is like a great ship, which carries the seven factors of awakening to cross over all, liberating one from craving and crossing the great ocean.
If one dons armor yet rides a donkey, one cannot enter among the great assembly;
but a person who dons armor and rides a horse or elephant will prevail over the enemy in the heat of battle.
The Dharma of the śrāvakas is like riding a donkey;
the Dharma of the bodhisattvas is like riding a horse or an elephant. Seated beneath the tree, they subdue the hosts of Māra and rescue those in the heavens and the world of men.
The void is filled with constellations, yet the multitude of stars does not illuminate the night;
when the moon alone emerges as the great light, men and women behold it with great joy.
The Dharma of the śrāvakas is like the stars;
the Dharma of the bodhisattvas is like the moon, shining alone. Through the grace of the bodhisattvas, all are brought to peace and security, and are led to give rise to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
In the darkness of night, the firefly’s glow is bright, yet people do not regard it as true light;
when the sun rises, its radiance is the great illumination, bringing benefit to Jambudvīpa.
The Dharma of the śrāvakas is like a firefly;
the wisdom of the bodhisattvas is like the sun and moon. As they traverse the ocean of birth and death to deliver beings, they manifest their brilliance to all people.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru heard the girl Viśākhā speak these verses and remained silent, not understanding what they meant.
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"These words are most extraordinary; what she speaks is without obstruction, and her wisdom is such as this."
"I wish to test you to see whether you can remain joyful and patient.
Śāriputra said to the girl Viśokā,
"In regard to the Three Vehicles, what do you seek to attain?"
The woman replied,
"One rides upon great compassion and great kindness regarding that which is sought.
Śāriputra replied:
"Do you seek the Mahāyāna-saṃnipāta?
The woman replied, "No."
Śāriputra asked again,
"Daughter, what do you seek by practicing this that you let out a lion’s roar?
The daughter replied to Śāriputra:
"In that which is sought, there is nothing to be sought; where there is something to be sought, one does not roar the lion's roar. Only by abiding nowhere can one roar the lion's roar.
Śāriputra, you have realized the truth through the Dharma—do you then possess the Dharma of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, or the Mahāyāna?"
Śāriputra replied, “No;
the characteristics of all dharmas are one and the same—empty and non-existent.
The woman asked Śāriputra:
"All dharmas are empty; by practicing what dharma do you establish the three vehicles?
Śāriputra replied to the woman, "By practicing nothing."
Śāriputra asked the woman again:
"Is there a difference between the existence of the Buddha-dharma and the non-existence of the Buddha-dharma?
The woman replied to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Is there a difference between near space and distant space?
Śāriputra replied, "There is no difference."
The woman asked Śāriputra:
"Is there a difference between internal emptiness and external emptiness?
He replied: "No."
“There is no difference. “In this way, Śāriputra,
the attainment of the Buddha-dharma and the non-attainment of the path-dharma are equal and without difference.”
The woman explained emptiness and the nature of emptiness to Śāriputra in various ways; Śāriputra remained silent, lacking any distinctive eloquence with which to refute or respond to these words.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the woman Viśākhā:
"What extraordinary essential teaching of the Tathāgata have you seen, such that it cannot be known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?"
The woman replied to the Venerable Maudgalyāyana:
"Are you able to know the number of stars in the trichiliocosm?
Maudgalyāyana replied to the woman:
"I shall enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and samādhi to contemplate the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*.
The woman said to Maudgalyāyana:
"The Tathāgata, by means of each individual samādhi, perceives the inclinations of the thoughts of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; how much more so, then, those of the stars?"
For this reason, it is known that the Tathāgata maintains mastery over all dharmas;
therefore, this is beyond the reach of knowledge for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Venerable Maudgalyāyana!
Do you know how many world-systems among the Buddha-fields of the ten directions are currently undergoing destruction,
and how many world-systems are currently undergoing formation?
He replied to the woman,
"I do not know.
The woman asked Maudgalyāyana again:
"How can one know how many Buddhas have passed away?
How many Buddhas are yet to come?
And how many Buddhas are presently residing?"
He replied to the woman,
“I do not know.
The woman asked Maudgalyāyana again:
“How many people in the world are lustful?
How many people take delight in anger?
And how many are deluded?”
"How many people practice all three matters?
How many people do not practice these three matters?
He replied:
"I do not know.
The woman asked the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana again:
"How many people in the world seek the path of the śrāvaka?"
"How many seek the path of the pratyekabuddha?
How many seek the Mahāyāna?
He replied to the woman:
“I do not know.
The woman asked Maudgalyāyana again:
“How many people in the world seek the path of the Buddha?”
How many do not believe in the Buddha-way?
How many believe in the ninety-six kinds of paths?
How many do not believe in the ninety-six kinds of paths?
"How many people are there who have no one to rely upon?
He replied, "I do not know."
The woman replied to Maudgalyāyana:
“The Tathāgata knows all these matters, and even more than this—immeasurable and limitless—beyond what can be known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”
Therefore, the Tathāgata maintains mastery over all dharmas.

Venerable Maudgalyāyana, who has been praised by the Tathāgata as the foremost in supernormal powers (ṛddhi), have you ever gone to the land of Gandhāra—translated into Chinese as the Land of Fragrant Purity?
"In this land there are trees adorned with the seven treasures, with various jewels forming their trunks and sandalwood providing their flowers and fragrance?
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to the girl, "This is something I have never heard before and never seen before;
it is only now that I hear the name of this buddha-field, which I have never before seen or heard."
"I wish to hear the names of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in this land, and whether they are currently preaching the Dharma there.
The woman replied, "The Buddha of that land is named Fragrant and Pure Radiance-Emitting Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha; he is preaching the Dharma in that land."
The woman Viśākhā, without rising from her seat, entered the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Auspicious Response) and reflected:
"When a Bodhisattva first resolves his mind to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he surpasses the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."

As my heart is sincere, I pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who is fragrant, pure, and radiates light—will manifest his radiance, enabling all the śrāvakas to see his buddha-field, and causing the fragrance of the sandalwood in that land to be smelled throughout this field.

When the woman Viśokā established this vow, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Gandhavairocanaprabhāsa immediately emitted light from his physical marks. All the śrāvakas in this world-system beheld that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Gandhavairocanaprabhāsa in that other land, preaching the Dharma among a great assembly of bodhisattvas; and all the śrāvakas there heard the Dharma being preached by that Buddha—all of this was through the grace of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.

That fragrant and pure Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha speaks with sixty kinds of tones—no different from what the woman Viśākhā has spoken—and those who first resolve their minds to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi are persons who surpass the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
When this was said, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From which buddha-field has this sandalwood fragrance come to reach this place, that its scent is thus?"
The Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:

"Because the maiden Viśākhā has uttered the lion’s roar together with the great śrāvakas, and because of this auspicious omen, the fragrance of sandalwood fills the Sahā world-system within that pure and fragrant Buddha-field where light is emitted."
The woman Viśākhā said to the Venerable Maudgalyāyana:
"If the Bodhisattva manifests such transformations of merit as these, how could he ever set his mind upon the Lesser Vehicle?"
The woman asked Maudgalyāyana again:
"Do you know how far Gandhāra is from here?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"I do not know," the woman said to Maudgalyāyana.

"Suppose this great trichiliocosm were filled with beings like you, Maudgalyāyana—like reeds, cane, bamboo, rice, grass, and trees—and let there be as many such Maudgalyāyanas as these; even after the passing of an eon, one could not calculate or know their number. Only after passing through that many Buddha-fields would one reach the realm governed by the Buddha Sugandhakūṭa-prabhāsa."
At that time, the Buddha Fragrant and Pure Radiance immediately withdrew his light and returned to his own land, whereupon that buddha-field no longer appeared.
Seeing this miraculous transformation, Maudgalyāyana remained silent, with nothing further to say or do.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the maiden Aśoka,
"Did you see the former Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
Can one see the Buddha’s form-body so that the Buddha might have something to say?
"Those who see my form, those who hear my voice— being foolish and lacking faith,
such people do not see [me]."
"One perceives the Buddha through the Dharma; the Buddha is the Dharma-body, and the Dharma is difficult to comprehend—it is for this reason that he cannot be seen.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa thought to himself:
"Has this girl ever seen Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
The woman replied to Kāśyapa:

“Indeed, I see the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; I do not see him with the fleshly eye, nor do I see him as form, nor do I see him as formlessness. Nor do I see him with the divine eye, nor do I see him with the eyes of sensation, perception, volition, consciousness, or cognition. Nor do I see him with the wisdom-eye, nor do I see him through conceptualization or discernment, nor do I see him with the Dharma-eye, nor do I see him as a body, nor do I see him as a Buddha-eye, nor do I see him as a life-principle.”
Mahākāśyapa! I see that the Tathāgata—for one such as the Venerable Mahākāśyapa—is the Great Illumination of non-existence.
He delights in birth within the world, considers himself to have a body, follows the practice of a pratyekabuddha, and contemplates desiring to see the Way.
Mahākāśyapa said to the woman:

"If this Dharma has no master, yet the foolish delight in birth, claiming 'this is my body' and 'all things are mine,' harboring the notion of a self within phenomena and failing to perceive them as neither internal nor external—whence could such a one be born through transformation?"
The woman said to Mahākāśyapa:
"All dharmas cannot be perceived; therefore, dharmas have no form.
Since they are thus imperceptible, how could they arise?"
Mahākāśyapa said to the woman,
"The Buddha-dharma is also empty and non-existent.
The woman replied again to Mahākāśyapa:
"One who wishes to see the unsurpassed, true, and correct Dharma should act in accordance with the Dharma.
Mahākāśyapa replied to the girl:
"I wish to hear even the teachings for laypeople; how much more so the Buddha-way, which I do not wish to leave unheard?"
The woman said to Mahākāśyapa,
"In the Dharma, one perceives neither existence nor non-existence.
Mahākāśyapa said to the woman:
"This dharma does not exist.
The woman spoke again to Mahākāśyapa:
"All dharmas are empty and have no form; they cannot be seen even through the truths."

If a son or daughter of good family wishes to see the physical marks of the Buddha’s body, they should purify their own conduct; by attaining purity in their conduct, they will perceive all forms of purity, and thus they will reach full maturity.
Mahākāśyapa asked the woman,
"What is it to purify one's own conduct until it reaches full maturity?
The woman replied to Mahākāśyapa:

"One who is able to contemplate the emptiness of their own body enters into the emptiness of all phenomena; since all phenomena neither decrease nor increase, this is called personally seeing all things as pure."
Mahākāśyapa said to the woman,
"What is meant by the emptiness of the body?
The woman replied:
"Emptiness is the exhaustion of emptiness;
this body is empty, and all dharmas are likewise empty.
Mahākāśyapa again asked the girl Viśokā:
"From what source did you hear this Dharma such that you are able to believe it as truth?
The Buddha has two causes and conditions for attaining faith:
hearing of the goodness of others and reflecting upon one's own conduct."
The woman replied to Kāśyapa:
"One may hear the teachings of others' wisdom, but one must observe for oneself the actions one performs.
The woman then addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"If one possesses personal wisdom and further contemplates all-encompassing wisdom, one takes clarity as one's teacher.
Mahākāśyapa replied to the girl:
"How does one know for oneself that one’s bodily conduct is virtuous?"
The woman replied:
"Hearing the Dharma and contemplating the good, one practices good with the body; thus one sees the cultivation of wholesome deeds.
Mahākāśyapa responded to the woman:
“How does a bodhisattva observe their own bodily conduct as virtuous?
The woman replied to Mahākāśyapa:
“When a bodhisattva’s Dharma is in harmony with all people in the world and not alienated from them, this is the bodhisattva’s virtuous bodily conduct.”
The woman replied again to Mahākāśyapa:
"Regarding future dharmas, past dharmas, and present dharmas, if the mind neither increases nor decreases, this is what it means to practice the Dharma of a bodhisattva."
Mahākāśyapa asked the girl,
"In what way do you see phenomena as neither increasing nor decreasing?
The girl replied to Mahākāśyapa:
“There are two things:
existence and non-existence, neither increasing nor decreasing. To form such a thought is to regard one’s own bodily and mental activities.
To see these bodily and mental activities, Mahākāśyapa, is to have nothing seen or known.”
She saw her own body.
Kāśyapa asked the woman,
“How did she see her own body?”
The woman replied,
"Mahākāśyapa has delivered himself alone and does not see any other people.
Mahākāśyapa answered:
“I see nothing,” the woman replied to Mahākāśyapa:
“All dharmas are such that there is neither anything to be relinquished nor anything to which one may become attached.”
Mahākāśyapa remained silent, unable to offer any reply.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, hearing these words—which he considered most difficult, indeed most difficult—took great joy and asked the girl Viśokā:
"From what source have you obtained such great benefit as to possess such eloquence?"
The woman replied to Subhūti:
“There is neither gain nor lack of gain.
Wisdom does not perceive dharmas, and dharmas do not perceive wisdom; there is neither internal contemplation nor external contemplation—this is wisdom.”
Why is this so? Subhūti,
that which is called "a dharma" is in fact not a dharma.
As for this, Venerable Subhūti!
Regarding the foremost dharma of delighting in secluded places—is it something that exists as a location, is there a teaching of it, and does it possess wisdom, or is it devoid of wisdom?
"Wisdom has nothing to be spoken.
Subhūti replied to the woman:
"One does not attain wisdom by means of either the state of seclusion or the state of having dharmas; this vision of dharmas is not something that can be spoken of, nor can it be expressed."
The woman replied to Subhūti:
"All dharmas are entirely like this: they cannot be seen and cannot be grasped. How, then, can one obtain great benefit and possess wisdom?"
Subhūti replied to the woman,
"If emptiness were devoid of wisdom, from what source would such a statement arise?
The woman asked Subhūti:
“Would one not hear an echo when there is a loud shout in the mountains?
All phenomena are exactly like this: faith is not called faith because it is an echo.
Whether there is wisdom or no wisdom, fundamentally there is no wisdom; it is an echo formed through the combination of sound.”
The woman asked Subhūti:
"Does this echo that issues forth have the form of a sound, or does it not?
He replied to the woman:
“An echo has no form or image; it exists as a name because of space.
All phenomena are like echoes, arising because of space.
The woman replied to Subhūti:
"All dharmas and all that is spoken of as dharmas arise from emptiness.
Subhūti asked the woman:
"If all dharmas arise from emptiness, for what reason does the Buddha say that there will be future Buddhas in the world as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?"
The woman replied to Subhūti:
"Do you wish to know the place from which dharmas arise?
He answered:
"If you wish to know:
'The place of birth is non-birth; non-birth is the place of birth,' Subhūti!"
Those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges do not see them departing from the Tathāgata, nor do they go anywhere; why is this so?
Because that which constitutes a Buddha does not arise from the initial resolve, nor does it cease with that resolve.
Subhūti replied to the woman, "This is called the foremost; it is unborn and unarisen.
The woman replied to Subhūti:
"All that is spoken is supreme; whether spoken or unspoken, it is likewise supreme.
All things are unborn and ineffable; this ineffability does not depart from the Buddha-dharma."
Subhūti replied to the woman, saying:

"It is most difficult; that one who dwells at home should cultivate the Way and yet possess such eloquence, having extensively studied the essentials of all things and deeply penetrated the subtle and profound."
The woman replied to Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva has neither the home life nor the life of renunciation; there is neither a śramaṇa nor one who is not a śramaṇa.”
"Why is this? Because one acts with mind and intention; for the practitioner, wisdom is supreme and discernment is virtuous.
Subhūti asked:
“How many dwelling places does a bodhisattva have?
I wish to hear your explanation.
The woman replied to Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva dwells by upholding eight dharmas; therefore, they abide in cessation.
Abiding wherever they dwell, there is nowhere they do not abide, and among śrāvakas, they are foremost.
What are these eight dharmas?”
1. Abiding as a bodhisattva, one constantly practices wholesome intentions, seeking the Buddha with a sincere heart without turning back or requiring further instruction;
and with great compassion, one rescues and protects those in the heavens and those on earth.
2. Not abandoning great compassion, remaining detached from worldly dharmas, and having no attachment to body or life; 3.
Fourth, practicing *upāyakauśalya*, they all resolve their minds to seek Buddhahood with incalculable wisdom;
constantly acting with vigor, they never tire of seeing and hearing as they seek all dharmas.
5. Fully knowing the spheres of conduct of bodhisattvas; 6.
Seventh, they intend to rescue all people;
their wisdom does not depend on others, as they personally realize and attain patience regarding all dharmas.
8. Thus it is, Subhūti!
One who practices by means of these eight dharmas surpasses all arhats and pratyekabuddhas wherever they may dwell.
Thereupon, Subhūti remained silent.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula asked the woman Viśākhā:

"Since you have attained such understanding, mastered the essential points, and possess the power of dhāraṇī and wisdom, why do you sit upon a golden couch, defiled and lacking a heart of humility and reverence, occupying a high seat while preaching the Dharma to the great bhikṣus?"
"I have heard the Buddha say:
'If a person is not ill, they must not sit on a high bed or lie down while listening to or preaching the Dharma.
" The woman replied to the Venerable Rāhula:
"How do you know what is considered pure and what is considered impure in the world?
Rāhula replied to the woman:
"In the world, those who uphold the precepts, have faith and acceptance, and do not transgress them are pure; if there are those who transgress, they are impure.
The woman replied to Rāhula:
"Stop! You have not yet understood, you have not yet comprehended."
Why is this so? Rāhula!
For one who upholds the precepts with faith and acceptance, refraining from transgression, that is impurity; whereas for one who transgresses the precepts, that is purity.
Why is this? Because when one does not rely on pure wisdom, there is purity; yet impurity is fundamentally non-existent, for there is neither purity nor impurity.
Such is the vision of the Arhats: that even those who have transgressed the precepts are pure.
Why is this so? Rāhula!

Because by being detached from precepts one no longer trains [in them], yet can reach infinite wisdom, remain far removed from the evil realms, and transcend the world; for this reason, it is called "detachment from precepts."
Rāhula replied to the woman:
"Is there any difference between that person who establishes a vow and one who does not establish a vow?
The woman replied:
"Venerable Rāhula!

Suppose one were to fashion various objects—such as bracelets, necklaces, or earrings—from refined gold. Would there be any difference between the color of that gold before it was fashioned and the color after it has been fashioned, whether the objects have already been made or not yet made?"
He replied, "There is no difference. "It is so, Rāhula!"
For what reason do you disdain sitting on a high bed and fail to practice respect and humility?
Rāhula, suffering has mental formations as its root.
"Formerly, the Bodhisattva sat upon a grass mat spread on the ground; this surpasses the sitting of the Śrāvakas and the sitting in the Brahma-heaven.
Rāhula asked again:
"In what way does his sitting surpass the sitting of the Śrāvakas and that in the Brahma-heaven?"
“Virtuous Rāhula!

When a bodhisattva sits upon grass beneath a tree, the Śakras, Brahmās, and Four Heavenly Kings of the trichiliocosm, as well as the people and great spirits from the world up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, all come to inquire after the bodhisattva’s welfare. Among them, some prostrate themselves with their heads at the bodhisattva’s feet, some kneel and bow, some offer salutations of courtesy, and some join their palms in reverence—is this not so?”
“Rāhula! Rāhula replied, “It is so, it is so.”
“Rāhula, you should know that when a bodhisattva dwells with a mind of high and low, it does not refer to physical seats; for this reason, he passes beyond the seats of the śrāvakas and the Brahmās.”
"You should understand it thus.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to the daughter Viśākhā:
"Do you not know?"

The Venerable Rāhula is of the lineage of the Cakravartin kings and is foremost among the honored; because he places his trust in the Way and its Virtue, from his youth he abandoned his home to become a śramaṇa, forsaking the kingdom of the Cakravartin.
"This is the son of Śākyamuni Buddha, foremost in the observance of the precepts.
Why do you, on the contrary, treat him with levity and fail to pay him due respect?
The woman said to the king:
"Stop; do not speak such words.
How could one compare a pearl of divine elixir to common crystal?
Has Your Majesty ever seen a lion give birth to a worm or a fox?"
"Could Prince Cakra possibly be the king of a minor kingdom?
The king replied, "No."
The woman spoke again to the king:
"You should know that for this reason, Rāhula was not born from the womb of a father and mother by means of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s lion-like conduct has subdued all ninety-six kinds of paths; he is fully endowed with the wisdom of supernormal powers and is a great sage of prowess. He thoroughly understands all dharmas without any obstruction, equally knows the thoughts in the minds of all people, and is fully cognizant of the future, the past, and the present. As a great King of Physicians, he heals the suffering and pain of humanity, and constantly exhorts and assists all in turning the Wheel of Dharma."
Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Revata, Rāhula, and Ānanda—though those of such standing hear the Dharma and practice it accordingly, they are still not yet sons of the Buddha.
At that time, while the venerable śrāvakas were among the great assembly, the woman preached the Dharma to them.
The woman said to the king:
"In the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara."
At that time, there was a Brahmin woman named Suradā—which in the language of Han means "Fresh and Pure Eloquence"—and also a Brahmin son named Vaidhara.
During the time of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, they took five stalks of flowers and scattered them over the Buddha.
At that time, the flower-seller gave rise to the aspiration, vowing to be husband and wife in every lifetime until they attained Buddhahood.
She further resolved to seek the Mahāyāna.
Thus, throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of the past, she had accumulated merit and made the vow to follow one another in every life, desiring to rescue those who were inferior.
Therefore, one should seek a vow from the Buddha;

seeking a vow from the Buddha will never be in vain. Ciñcā, a woman of the Śākya clan, having generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through great joy and the practice of *upāya-kauśalya*, exhorted all bodhisattvas to manifest as having wives, children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, gold, silver, precious jewels, and *maṇi* pearls.
Why is this? It is to protect the ninety-six kinds of paths and not to allow them to slander the Bodhisattva as being no true man, lest the King be born as a eunuch.
What is so extraordinary about this world that one would speak of enduring such diligent suffering?
If one were to entertain such a thought, one would fall into the hells, where the suffering day and night is beyond description.
Since the Bodhisattva received his prediction from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, he has been free from any conceptualization of form.
The woman said to the king:

"At that time, the Brahmin’s son Vaidhurya obtained the light of wisdom from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara; he attained sixty thousand gates of samādhi and reached inexhaustibility, clearly understanding as many dharmas of the Dhāraṇīs as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
Upon receiving this at another time, he completely abandons all that was previously vowed and all that was formerly practiced, from the attainment of *kṣānti*.
Some say:
"Rāhula is the son of the Buddha; he was born from the womb of his parents."
To say this is to slander the Tathāgata.

A bodhisattva does not regard wife or children, nor kingdom or city, for the sake of the pleasures of form; the bodhisattva is detached from craving and desire, remaining untainted by worldly dharmas.
The woman said to the king:
"One might still find fire by searching within the great ocean, but one cannot find greed, lust, hatred, or anger in a bodhisattva.

Your Majesty should know this dharma: the Venerable Rāhula was born through transformation; he was not born from the womb of a mother and father, and all that he manifested was through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha."

The Bodhisattva follows worldly customs in order to teach and transform others, guarding against all deluded thoughts. Manifesting forms like illusions, he never departs from samādhi in whatever he does. He manifests among children, among laymen in white robes, among bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, among gods and humans, and among humans and non-humans; whether among the noble or the lowly, the old or the young, the base or the common, among musicians, palace ladies, wine, or food—he is born wherever he wishes to deliver beings according to their needs.
"In this way, the places where he manifests himself are incalculable and innumerable.
Within the assembly, there arose those who thought:
"Who among us is truly a son of the lineage of the Tathāgata?"

“Those who possess equal knowledge and right view, who do not sever the Three Jewels, who protect the seven factors of enlightenment, and who transform others according to their inclinations—such people as these are truly the sons of the Buddha.”
"If good sons or good daughters wish to become true children of the Buddha, they should resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When these words were spoken, twenty-five women from the king's inner palace all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, having heard the Lion’s Roar of the girl Viśokā, the thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and simultaneously raised their voices, saying:
"We are the supreme sons of the Buddhas of the future and the Buddhas of the past."
Having thus resolved her mind, she rained down celestial flowers that completely covered the great city of Rājagṛha as an offering to the woman Viśākhā.
Then Viśākhā, from beneath the golden couch, stepped forward toward the venerable śrāvakas.
The woman Viśokā asked the venerable śrāvakas:
"Are you proficient in the dharma of alms-gathering?
The venerable śrāvakas replied to the woman:
"I have understood.
"How have you understood? He replied:

“The body has four spirits that arise from causes and conditions; they constantly cover and transform it in accordance with its nature, fearing its destruction. For this reason, one must provide it with food and drink. This body is established by means of food and drink; without food and drink, it cannot find peace.”
This body is like a dilapidated cart that must be provided with grease and oil to achieve stability.

For this reason, one seeks food at the proper time in order to protect the body; yet one does not practice begging out of self-conceit, nor for the sake of physical appearance, nor out of greed, but rather because one desires to destroy greed.
When the woman Viśākhā heard the various venerable śrāvakas each speak of these matters, she neither rejoiced nor grieved at what was said:
"Such is this body, fraught with calamity and affliction; its suffering is thus."
He immediately invited all the śrāvakas at that time and provided them with a meal of a hundred flavors.
When the meal was finished, they all exchanged polite greetings and said:
"Let us return to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to listen to the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma; we shall all go together."

After her meal, the woman Viśākhā, together with her parents, brothers, kinsmen, the ladies of the inner palace, the ministers, and the common people, went out of the city to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain. She approached the Buddha, prostrated herself with her head at his feet in salutation, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The various venerable śrāvakas arose from their meditative absorption and all came to pay homage to the Buddha, sitting to one side.
Śāriputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The discourse delivered by this woman, Aśoka, is most difficult; she has entered the profound essentials of the Dharma and, through the practice of skillful means, has established countless people. She is fully capable of answering every kind of question posed to her."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“This girl, Free from Sorrow (Aśoka), has made offerings to ninety-two billion buddhas and performed meritorious deeds, never being separated from upāyakauśalya.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
"For what reason does this woman not relinquish her female form?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If the śrāvakas were to ask, 'Is this one without sorrow a woman?

and if they, not having deeply entered the Prajñāpāramitā and not having perceived the faculties of others, observe both the fundamental and the manifest and thus regard what is practiced with equanimity."

The Bodhisattva, expressing her joy and delight, manifested herself as both male and female through the power of skillful means, being entirely free from any obstruction, for the purpose of delivering both men and women.
The woman Viśākhā, wishing to resolve Śāriputra’s doubts, manifested her true form and made this vow:
"May everyone in this great assembly see me as a man."
Having had this thought, the great assembly immediately saw that Aśoka was no longer a woman, but a man; they no longer saw the form of a woman.
At that moment, Aśoka leapt into the air to a height of seventy *zhang* above the ground and remained suspended in mid-air.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you see this Man of No Grief, leaping into the air at a height of seventy *zhang* above the ground? Do you see him?"
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha,
“Indeed, I have seen it.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"This Aśoka shall become a Buddha after seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas; the Buddha’s name shall be Vighuṣṭa (translated into Chinese as 'Free from Sorrow'), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. His buddha-field shall be named Vimalaprabhājvālā (translated into Chinese as 'Stainless Radiant Light'), and his lifespan shall be one hundred thousand kalpas."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the sutras and Dharma shall remain for ten kalpas without interruption.
In this land, the ground is entirely like fine lapis lazuli.
In each of the eight directions of that buddha-field, there is a single path, which is the place where the Buddha travels.

The trees were made of the seven precious gems; the railings were made of various jewels; celestial silks formed the canopies; and it was perfumed with famous incenses. There were no foul stones, sands, or rubble; everything was composed purely of precious jewels.
Within that land there are no hells, animals, or hungry ghosts; there are only bodhisattvas, devas, and humans, resembling the palace where the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven dwells.
At that time, the great assembly and King Ajātaśatru were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, all exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!

Then, the principal consort of King Ajātaśatru, whose name was Cīrāhvayā (translated into Chinese as Yuèmíngzhào, meaning Moon-Bright-Illumination), rose from her seat, joined her palms, marveled at her own heart, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since it is already difficult to have attained human birth, and since I further cherish and nourish this Bodhisattva, my joy is redoubled; by virtue of this merit, I resolve my mind to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
He made this resolve and aspiration:

"Now that the Buddha has granted the Bodhisattva Aśoka the prophecy of future Buddhahood, when that kalpa comes to an end, I vow that I shall follow in his footsteps and attain Buddhahood within that same buddha-field."
At that time, the Buddha knew the aspiration in the heart of King Śrīmatī’s wife.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you see King Śrīmatī’s wife?"
Śāriputra said, “I see it.

“The consort of the king, Candraprabhā, by virtue of these meritorious deeds, shall cast off her female body; having attained a male body, she shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as a deity named Ratnottamā.”
When Maitreya Buddha descends, there will be a king named Aha who shall serve as his crown prince; his name will be Zhonghao, and he shall provide offerings to Maitreya for the remainder of his life.
In the future, he shall become a śramaṇa under Maitreya; he will uphold the superior Dharma, he will uphold the middling Dharma, and he will also uphold the inferior Dharma.
He will collectively make offerings to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas during this Bhadrakalpa, and furthermore, he will practice the Bodhisattva path.
After this Tathāgata Viśoka has attained Buddhahood, Ratnaprathamamati shall become a Cakravartin king in that same realm, named Ratnasaṃpatti.

He shall serve and attend upon the Tathāgata for as long as his life lasts, and by following that Buddha, he shall subsequently attain Buddhahood, becoming the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Samantaprabhāsa.
Since this teaching is the original land of the stainless, pure, and radiant realm, its circumstances are no different from those of the domain governed by the Tathāgata Vigatāśoka.

When the King’s consort Candraprabhā heard the Buddha speak of these additional benefits, she leaped for joy all the more; sighing over her own body with gratitude, she offered to the Buddha a maṇi jewel worth a million taels of gold.
From King Ajātaśatru, he requested to uphold the five precepts; he established a separate residence where he abstained from sexual conduct, causing all to practice purity.
Then, the Bodhisattva Aśoka descended from the midst of the void and stood before the Buddha with palms joined, saying:

"May it be that when I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas within my land shall spontaneously manifest and grow upon great Dharma thrones; may the kāṣāya robes be naturally worn upon their bodies, such that there is no distinction between old and young, and they possess the appearance of those twenty years of age."
"Now I vow to become a śramaṇa myself; may I spontaneously don the dharma robes.
At that very moment, he manifested that appearance.
The Bodhisattva Aśoka then addressed the king:

“Dharmas are not solid; they stand upon emptiness and sit upon emptiness. Amidst mindfulness and non-mindfulness, one maintains the mind without distraction. There is nothing to be recorded, and whatever is done has no point of attachment.”
"Does the King see this?
Within a single day, I have become a woman, transformed into the form of a man, and again appeared as a bhikṣu-saṃgha.
Which of these is truly the reality, and which is otherwise?"
Within the human body there are the three poisons; by means of the three medicines, these poisons are treated until they are completely consumed.
Knowing this Dharma, Great King, you should not engage in unrighteous conduct.
You should frequently go to the Buddha and the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, who can remove the defilements of men, increase their merit, and deliver those who have not yet been delivered.
"The kingdom has many affairs; you may depart as you please.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "The Bodhisattva No-Grief-and-Sorrow has received his prediction, understands the truths, is able to uphold them, and is able to expound them; he shall extensively preach the Dharma for the sake of all beings."

If there are good men or good women who wish to seek the Buddha-way, even if they were to take this trichiliocosm filled with the seven treasures and offer it to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, it would not equal the merit of hearing this sutra, believing it, and not slandering it—whose merit is incalculable; how much more so for those who practice it and provide offerings of silk, flowers, banners, canopies, and flags throughout their entire lives?
"The merit thereof cannot be calculated.

Having received these instructions, the bhikṣus were uplifted; the Bodhisattva Aśoka rejoiced; King Ajātaśatru, Queen Candraprabhā, the venerable bhikṣu Ānanda, the entire great assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, spirits, and asuras, all rejoiced upon hearing the Buddha preach this sutra. They then prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground before the Buddha in salutation and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Bodhisattva Ajita, Daughter of King Ajātaśatru.
